NOTE: This section is background to help you understand programming. You will work with pre-existing code and clear instructions for edits. You will not be tested on coding in quizzes or exams. The goal is to help you feel more familiar and confident using computer code to explore the calculus models in this class. This is a marimo notebook: it mixes Python code with Markdown to make code and text look aesthetic. Run a code cell with the play button; marimo updates dependent cells automatically. Use the controls below to explore models without editing their implementation. Your answers still belong on your worksheet. Here, Python executes Euler's method rapidly to simulate the dynamics of biological systems.

Within a code cell, write Python. Python can act as a calculator. A # starts a comment.

Variable assignment and vectors

The real power of code is assigning values to variables. Python uses =. NumPy arrays are numerical vectors; for example, np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]). Multiplication by a scalar acts on each element of an array. Read the following code, then run the code and check the results. Is the product what you expected?

Simulating viral dynamics using Euler's Method

Python lets us do many long calculations even faster than Google Sheets! Let's explore how viral load decays over time.

A protease inhibitor-treated patient

We'll begin by considering a patient who has been treated with protease inhibitors, so that their viral production p is temporarily 0. ||[V' = \frac{dV}{dt} = p-cV = 0-cV = -cV.||]Euler's method adds small changes calculated using ||(V'||): ||[V_{i+1}=V_i+(t_{i+1}-t_i)(p-cV_i).||]You've practiced this in Google Sheets. Use ||(c=0.3256||) per day (the source's average for three patients), ||(V_0=185000||) particles per mL, and one-day steps.

Speeding up our calculation

While not as bad as writing out calculations by hand, having four lines of code for every calculation doesn’t seem very efficient! That’s where for loops come in. These are programming tools that let us repeat calculations many times. Let’s rewrite our last three calculations in a for loop. Look over the comments on the code and see if you can recognize how the calculation repeats itself. Python counts positions from zero, so position 0 holds the initial value.
